title: Can LLMs Reason Soundly in Law? Auditing Inference Patterns for Legal Judgment
claim: A model's output can be decomposed into interaction patterns, and separating reliable from unreliable ones exposes flawed reasoning behind correct outputs.
layout: Dense left-to-right interaction trees, with right-side inset panels and a bottom input text
description: A dense annotated figure on a white background. The left and center show a large tree-like list of interaction effects. Each entry gives a value such as R^AND = 0.4732 or U^OR = 0.0609, with small phrase boxes below it, for example "chased", "with an axe", "bit". A thick blue bracket labelled "Reliable interaction effects" covers the left columns and a thick red bracket labelled "Unreliable interaction effects" covers the right. A "+" node joins them, and a blue double-line equals sign links them to the "LLM's output v('Assault'|x)" label. Phrase boxes use a colour code: green for relevant, grey for irrelevant and orange for forbidden. At the top right, a small transformer diagram sits between two arrows, with the input legal case below it. A dashed inset plots the LLM's output scores against the AND-OR model's scores over masked inputs. The bottom has the legal case text with phrases highlighted.
caption: {Correctness of the detailed inference patterns of an LLM. The AND-OR logical model $h(\cdot)$ accurately fits the output score of the LLM $v(\cdot)$ when making the judgment "Assault" for Andy, $h($"Assault"$|x) = v($"Assault"$|x)$, no matter how the input legal case $x$ is masked in the bottom-right figure. Blue edges connect reliable interaction effects ($R^{\rm AND}_S$ and $R^{\rm OR}_S$) that contribute to the output score $v($"Assault"$|x)$, typically aligning with legal domain knowledge. Red edges connect unreliable interaction effects ($U^{\rm AND}_S$ and $U^{\rm OR}_S$) that contribute to $v($"Assault"$|x)$, often reflecting problematic patterns used by the LLM for the judgment.}
abstract: This paper presents a method to analyze the inference patterns used by Large Language Models (LLMs) for judgment in a case study on legal LLMs, so as to identify potential incorrect representations of the LLM, according to human domain knowledge. Unlike traditional evaluations on language generation results, we propose to evaluate the correctness of the detailed inference patterns of an LLM behind its seemingly correct outputs. To this end, we quantify the interactions between input phrases used by the LLM as primitive inference patterns, because recent theoretical achievements have proven several mathematical guarantees of the faithfulness of the interaction-based explanation. We design a set of metrics to evaluate the detailed inference patterns of LLMs. Experiments show that even when the language generation results appear correct, a significant portion of the inference patterns used by the LLM for the legal judgment may represent misleading or irrelevant logic.
